source.title: Sparsity and Superposition in Mixture of Experts
source.authors: Marmik Chaudhari; Jeremi Nuer; Rome Thorstenson

page_placements.theme: Toy models: where superposition and polysemanticity come from, and their geometry

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on superposition and monosemanticity in synthetic toy MoEs, but it does not measure neuron-pole job shares, explain real model neurons, or test any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures feature representation and interference in synthetic toy networks, not the listed versions’ neuron-pole explanation shares or tests. Its own MoE-versus-dense results are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited prior-work results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Toy autoencoder MoE vs dense models on synthetic features, measuring superposition (features per dimension, interference), not neuron explanation shares. No language-model neurons, InceptionV1, attribution graphs or explanation scoring. The paper says 'more monosemantic' means less superposition, not basis-aligned neurons. The MoE-versus-dense result touches the architecture theme of V4 only loosely, so it is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors claim toy MoEs reach comparable loss while being more interpretable. They frame this as challenging a supposed interpretability-capability tension, though the dense model's loss is lower at every sparsity. They also note the methods do not scale naturally to large models.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic sparse-feature inputs and toy MoE reconstruction models, measuring feature-weight geometry and superposition rather than explaining real model neurons or testing explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with feature sparsity, feature importance, number of experts/network sparsity, architecture, routing top-k, and router initialization. The paper reports a mixed transition region for some MoE settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic toy models with equal total parameters, MoEs showed fewer features per dimension than dense models, and superposition fell as expert count rose. Dense models kept lower reconstruction loss (gap about 0.03–0.08).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy reconstruction models, MoE routing (network sparsity) reduces superposition relative to dense models, at a small loss cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense toy models showed sharp phase changes across feature sparsity and importance. MoE transitions were more continuous, with a mixed region around sparsity 0.48–0.7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, increasing network sparsity softens superposition phase changes.

fits_no_version.finding: The features initially routed to an expert were represented more monosemantically by it; with uniform importance they averaged 1.03 SD below the expert's mean superposition score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy MoEs, router initialization shapes which features an expert represents monosemantically.

record.problems: All experiments use controlled toy models and synthetic feature distributions. The authors say transfer to realistic transformer MoEs is uncertain and that the methods do not scale naturally to larger models. Several plots do not provide exact numerical values in the text; some results select the lowest-loss model from ten runs per cell. Downstream performance trade-offs and large-scale specialization dynamics are not evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: Section 6, Table 1 reports expert usage statistics by monosemantic-feature count for Xavier and k-hot initializations; omitted because usage conditional on feature activation is not a neuron-pole job-share or explanation test. Appendix A.4 routing and loss examples are also omitted as they concern toy-model routing and reconstruction loss rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job shares.
No real language models, dense or MoE, and no scale sweep; only synthetic toy reconstruction models.
No InceptionV1 neurons, cat-and-car example or pose analysis.

No measured share of interpretable neurons in real models, no tool comparison and no vision-model estimates. The toy MoE superposition reduction is architecture-related but measures feature interference, not neuron interpretability.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No neuron explanations tested against held-out activations.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. States on R3–R6 and R8–R11 describe the paper's own toy findings, not any claim version. Relation is 'discusses' only in the broad sense that the paper concerns superposition and polysemanticity; it does not mention the essay or the OpenAI neuron-explanation work.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or estimates of single-job, two-job, or unexplained shares.
No language models, model-scale sweep, or shares of interpretable neuron poles; the experiments use synthetic toy models.
No InceptionV1 neurons, cat-and-car example, or pose interpretation.
No late-layer neuron audit, comparison of explanation tools, or InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model.
No explanations tested for prediction of neuron activations on held-out examples.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

relation.reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and superposition in toy models but doesn't test any version of the claim.

tranche.reason: Toy MoE autoencoders on synthetic features measure superposition (features per dimension, interference). There are no real-model neurons, explanations or scoring. This is a related but different construct, so the study neither tests nor uses the claim.

source_check.notes: The paper says 'more monosemantic' means less superposition, not basis-aligned neurons (Section 3). So no row bears on neuron-pole job shares (V1/V2) or on V4's interpretable-neuron share. The authors note the dense model's loss is lower at every sparsity and that their methods do not scale to large models.

statements.correction: Matches the text. With equal total parameters, the dense model (n=100, m=20) has more features per dimension than the MoEs, and this falls as expert count rises (4, 10, 20 experts). Dense loss is lower at every sparsity, by about 0.03-0.08, and the gap narrows as expert count rises. These are toy autoencoders on synthetic features.
